key_insight: This audit found no robust racial or sex differences in pain recommendations, while variation across models and settings was much larger.
clinical_relevance: Clinical AI fairness assessments should test each deployed configuration because aggregate findings may obscure substantial differences in treatment recommendations.
method: Study 1 tested four open-weight LLMs on six acute-pain vignettes, varying race, sex and explicit versus name-cued identity.
Identity comparisons were paired with a White male reference using the same case and sampling seed.
Study 2 evaluated 24 configurations of 17 models on the same vignettes and 50 clinician-written Q-Pain cases.
evidence_signal: No Study 2 comparison survived false-discovery-rate correction across 1,386 tests; all pain-severity differences met equivalence bounds of ±1 point on a 0–10 scale.
watch_item: These exploratory, single-prompt results do not establish absence of bias: opioid estimates were less precise, and Study 1 could not exclude differences of about 20 percentage points.
paper_title: Do Large Language Models Show Racial and Sex Bias in Pain Management? A Counterfactual Audit of GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama, DeepSeek and Qwen
